 So I was 20 and going back and forth about killing myself. Eventually putting a rifle in my mouth. I spent 2 hours trying to stop myself until I fell asleep crying. I decided to wait a while because I didn't think it was a good time because I cared about my family and didn't want to kill myself during my sister's pregnancy with my niece. So a few weeks later my friend (who didn't know I was suicidal) asked if I wanted to do acid with him at his house with a few of our other friends. I said sure I didn't really have any experience with psychedelics at that point. so he recommended doing 1 but from my experience with other drugs I usually need more that a regular amount because my body is resistant to almost every drug. 
 So we get to my friend's house in Bellingham, WA and we settle in and decide to all drop at the same time. We had 2 people trip sit because there were like 5 of us taking it. So we all grab one tab and take it together. It tastes metallic. I was super nervous. We all sit down and smoke some weed and turn on some Bonobo and Nujabes. Like 45 minutes go by and the trip commences. We all feel weird. Breathing feels amazing. My spinal cord is super tingly. The popcorn ceiling is crawling. Everything is bright colored and music can be felt. I remember feeling like the world was truly beautiful, even the man made stuff. I remember seeing beauty in architecture, plants, clothing, food. Looking in mirror I could see every layer of skin on my body and thought how amazing it is I was even born. I started sondering on and on about the size of the universe and the chances at life occurring. I felt one with the earth. I felt like I finally belonged. We started playing music in my friend's garage. I've never heard such beautiful music than the cacophony of sounds my friend's played that day. It's a shame we weren't sober enough to record it. Mind you this was only the first 2 hours. We decided we could handle taking more so we each took 1 to 2 more tabs each. At this point we really wanted to get out of the house so we decided to take a hike around Bellingham and tour the college campus (it was late summer so the school was still closed). Trees were extra green. The sky was cloudy and it was sprinkling on and off. The grass was beautiful. It was like being in a video game. We walked on a trail that takes you to an overlook a few hundred feet above the city. The distance walked felt like nothing. Rain on my face felt great. The city from the overlook was shimmering. All the lights were pulsing to my heart beat. I was one with the world. We walked back home and started to come down a little bit just as we were getting home. It was really dark but we didn't care. We got home and put on some Canadian movie I can't remember. 
 Eventually we started winding down and decided to go to bed. It took like 4 hours but I fell asleep as the sun was rising. We all woke up around 9 and felt more tired than I've ever felt. We smoked a bunch of weed and listened to some more chill music. We talked about our trip and all agreed that was one of the most positive experiences of our lives.

What I learned: We are all together in this world. Everyone is going through shit too. Life is with living, simply because we're all lucky to have been born. Life is a journey not a destination. Reality is what you perceive. You see what you want to see. That includes positive and negative. Emotions are chemical reactions to your surroundings. You choose how to react to your situations. You choose to feel happy. You choose to be sad. You choose to feel offended. You choose to feel shame or embarrassment. Your ego/self is what's holding you back from feeling happy. If you want to be happy then choose to be happy no matter your situation or past trauma. Choose happiness.

As always may the force be with you, Zeke.

In another thread someone asked how the US is or is not a free market. I provided many examples showing how the US is not a free market. I received a negative downvote, for what I assume is someone venting partisan rage in an unproductive way.

My examples are located here , but Id love to hear your opinions (on what is really a definition).
What is your definition of a free market?
A capitalist market with minimal regulations to protect the consumer, protect small businesses, and stop too-big-to-fail.

A market in which private property rights are protected, prices are set and resources are allocated in response to supply and demand, companies compete on their own merits, and the government does not interfere and pick winners and losers.

The United States isn't a free market. There are a number of regulations which restrict what businesses can do, there are barriers to entry, there are subsidies, and a slew of other non-laissez faire programs in place. I think it's safe to say we're more of a free market than not, but we're a mixed economy.

A truly free market may not be possible, but we can certainly have much much freer markets.

Most people seem to think of a free market as one with the MINIMUM of government intervention and a flat to neutral rule setting. I.E. the rules aren't written to in a manner that allows them to favor particular business sectors or individual businesses.

Example of government playing games with the playing field

http://www.ibtimes.co.uk/travelling-work-work-european-court-rules-1519285

Many consulting or service businesses will have personnel go directly to worksites. Under these rules they have to either charge more or adopt a less efficient model. Either way they going to be less viable as businesses, while their competitors are rewarded.

I had a significant conversation about this with Brother_Tempus here.

My POV in a nutshell: pure market economies can't exist because agents in the market circumvent market forces via collusion, monopoly, price-setting, etc. The U.S. has a mixed economy, like all successful economies in the modern world, a market with rules set by the government, but we're nowhere near a pure command economy, which haven't worked well historically (just like unregulated--so called free--markets haven't).

"Free Market" isn't a binary issue with some convenient check boxes. It's a gradient.

On one side of the scale, we have a market which is so encumbered by regulation that it is nearly impossible to do business. I kind of doubt anyone wants this. It's impractical.

In a completely free market, I'd be able to slaughter your children and sell their meat while labelling it as organic tofu. I kind of doubt anyone wants this. It's impractical.

When someone says "The US is not a free market", clearly they have the economic background of a retarded redneck who learned about the economy by sucking the cock of another retarded redneck. Why? Because holding a "Pure Free Market" up as an ideal is impractical.

What we have is a "Mixed Economy" and almost everyone is going to be willing to make some sacrifices of freedom in order to have some protections. Else, their children might end up on their plate. Throwing terms like, "Free Market" around isn't productive. What we need to focus on are what aspects we are willing to regulate and which aspects we will keep free.
